Dermatology · published research

Skin aging/rejuvenation

PBM may improve selected short-term facial wrinkle measures; the largest numerical estimate comes from a meta-analysis of six studies, while individual trials report improvements on some measures but not others. Evidence is less certain for crow’s feet, hydration and elasticity, and very uncertain for persistence after treatment.

Summary of the Evidence

Photobiomodulation may improve short-term facial wrinkle outcomes with some tested light protocols, but results vary across studies and outcome measures. Certainty is low to moderate for wrinkle outcomes, low for crow’s-feet, hydration, and elasticity, and very low for benefits lasting after treatment ends. Laboratory and animal findings provide biological context but do not resolve these clinical uncertainties.

Human and clinical evidence

The clinical literature includes direct sham-controlled facial studies and active or uncontrolled comparisons, with variation in measures and regimens. The 2018 systematic review identified six skin-rejuvenation randomized trials and assigned an Oxford recommendation Grade C. The 2023 meta-analysis pooled six studies to estimate wrinkle outcomes (Jagdeo et al. 2018; Le Ngoc et al. 2023).

In a 2007 split-face, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 112 participants were randomized to red, near-infrared, combined-light or control conditions, and 76 completed the study. Wrinkle and elasticity findings favored treated sides, with follow-up extending three months after the course (Lee et al. 2007).

A newer sham-controlled trial in 95 women compared red LED three times weekly, twice weekly or sham for four weeks. Blinded clinician ratings on the Wrinkle Assessment Scale did not differ, while image analysis favored light for selected wrinkle locations and satisfaction favored both active schedules (Bragato et al. 2025).

A multicenter double-blind trial in 60 Asian adults compared a home mask combining 630-nm red and 850-nm near-infrared with sham for 16 weeks. Independent raters and investigators found crow’s-feet grade differences favoring the active arm at weeks 8, 12 and 16 (Park et al. 2025).

A randomized split-face study in 137 women compared amber and red PBM, not light with sham. Wrinkle volume fell after treatment on both active sides, while hydration and viscoelasticity did not improve (Mota et al. 2023).

In a 30-person active wavelength comparison, 570-nm yellow plus red and near-infrared light was compared with 590-nm yellow plus red and near-infrared light. Both groups improved from baseline, and the 570-nm group did better after treatment on some scores. This comparison cannot show an effect versus no PBM (Yi et al. 2025).

A single-arm home-mask study in 20 participants reported changes in wrinkles and other skin-quality measures, but included no control group (Kim et al. 2026a). Another 33-person comparison combined micro-LED with polynucleotide injections, so its results cannot be attributed to light alone (Kim et al. 2026b).

A randomized trial adding low-level laser to radiofrequency did not show additional wrinkle benefit over radiofrequency alone (Pereira et al. 2016).

Animal evidence

In naturally aged mice, daily 630–635-nm red light at 8 J/cm² for 28 days improved dermal thickness and smoothness compared with green or white light (Chang et al. 2025).

In UVB-photoaged mice, 625–630-nm organic LED at 6 or 10 J/cm² increased collagen density and reduced wrinkles and roughness compared with UVB-only controls (Lee et al. 2024).

In hairless mice, 595-nm yellow or 630-nm red LED produced dose-dependent collagen I increases compared with controls, with changes observed through 21 days (Kim et al. 2016).

In UVB-photoaged mice, human adipose-derived stem cells preconditioned with 650-nm light at 4 J/cm² were associated with a thinner epidermis and thicker dermis. This is cell-transfer evidence rather than direct skin PBM (Liao et al. 2018).

Rats received an 800-nm diode laser at 20, 40 or 60 J/cm² or no irradiation. Dermal thickness increased, and 40 J/cm² increased collagen markers (Dang et al. 2011).

In mice, 800-nm diode exposures at 20–60 J/cm² caused thermal injury followed by collagen remodeling. This thermal-laser experiment is not PBM (Ren et al. 2016).

Hairless mice received Q-switched 1064-nm Nd:YAG at 0.5–2 J/cm² or no irradiation. Lower-dose exposure increased collagen and dermal thickness (Yang et al. 2019).

KM mice were treated with 595-nm pulsed-dye, 1064-nm Q-switched or 1320-nm Nd:YAG lasers. The 1064-nm treatment best improved mechanics, while 1320 nm improved barrier and water-holding measures. These are laser resurfacing models, not direct PBM comparisons (Dang et al. 2006).

Guinea pigs and ex-vivo pig skin received a 755/808/1064-nm thermal laser. Triple wavelengths increased collagen and epidermal thickness compared with 1064 nm, with thermal damage also measured (Lee et al. 2025).

UVB-injured mice received 630-nm 5-ALA photodynamic therapy. Roughness, epidermal thickness and collagen improved, but photodynamic therapy is distinct from PBM (Shi et al. 2026).

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

Human skin-cell experiments report changes in collagen, elastin and cellular energy after red and near-infrared light; these mechanistic outcomes do not establish patient benefit (Li et al. 2021).

An ex-vivo UVB-damaged human skin model reported broader marker recovery with micro-LED plus polynucleotide than with polynucleotide alone. The combined treatment prevents attributing the result to light alone (Kim et al. 2026b).

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

Human facial protocols include yellow or amber light around 570–590 nm, red light around 630–660 nm, and near-infrared light around 830–850 nm. Studies applied light to the face or periocular area using clinic systems and home masks. Reported fluence includes 3.8 J/cm² for an amber/red split-face comparison and 8.05 J/cm² for a red mask trial. The 2007 trial reported 66 J/cm² for red and 126 J/cm² for near-infrared treatment. These regimens and devices are not directly interchangeable.

Schedules range from two or three sessions weekly for four weeks, to ten sessions over four weeks, to home use five times weekly for 12 weeks. A 16-week mask trial reported maximum output of 10 mW/cm² for each of its red and near-infrared channels. Outcomes include clinician wrinkle grading, image-based wrinkle length, profilometry, wrinkle volume, skin texture, hydration and elasticity. No direct comparison establishes an optimal wavelength, dose or schedule.

The animal literature spans red and near-infrared light, but also includes cell transfer, thermal laser exposure and photodynamic therapy. These models should not be combined into one PBM treatment range or used as direct evidence for human rejuvenation.

Interpretation

Clinical findings support possible short-term improvement in selected facial wrinkle outcomes with some tested light protocols. Results differ across clinician ratings, digital measures and active wavelength comparisons. Evidence for hydration, elasticity and benefit after treatment ends is less consistent. Animal and laboratory findings support biological plausibility but do not substitute for controlled patient outcomes. A single estimate should not be generalized to all wavelengths, devices or skin-aging outcomes.

Clinical effect sizes (estimate)

Facial wrinkle outcomes — Le Ngoc et al. (2023) pooled six studies with 268 participants: standardized mean difference (SMD) −3.45 (95% CI −3.84 to −3.06; I²=33%). The estimate combines different wrinkle measures and should be read cautiously because the review flags possible missing studies and has inconsistent wording about statistical significance.

Wrinkle severity — In Lee et al. (2007), 76 of 112 randomized participants completed follow-up. At three months after treatment, mean improvement from baseline was 26% with 633-nm red light, 33% with 830-nm near-infrared, and 36% with both; the sham side showed no change. These are within-trial changes, not a pooled estimate.

Crow’s feet — Park et al. (2025) reported independent-rater improvement in 86.2% of the active group and a 69.5% improvement-rate difference versus sham in the full-analysis set after 16 weeks. This preserves the article’s wording and is not converted to percentage points.

Periocular wrinkle volume — Mota et al. (2023) reported reductions of 31.6% on the red-light side and 29.9% on the amber-light side after ten sessions over four weeks. Both sides received active light, so this does not estimate PBM versus sham or no treatment.

Elasticity and hydration — Lee et al. (2007) reported maximum mean elasticity improvements at three months of 14% with red, 19% with near-infrared and 16% with combined treatment, with no change on sham. Mota et al. (2023) found no improvement in hydration or viscoelasticity.

Uncontrolled wrinkle count — Kim et al. (2026a) reported up to a 27.22% decrease after 12 weeks with a home-use near-infrared mask in a 20-person single-arm study. This is a within-group change without a control comparison.

Certainty of evidence (estimate)

Low-to-moderate for short-term facial wrinkle outcomes with tested LED protocols. Jagdeo et al. 2018 assigned Oxford recommendation Grade C. Le Ngoc et al. 2023 adds a pooled estimate but flags possible missing studies and gives inconsistent wording about statistical significance. Newer sham-controlled trials also differ by outcome.

Low for crow’s-feet improvement with the tested red and near-infrared mask. Support comes mainly from one multicenter sham-controlled trial without independent replication.

Low for hydration and elasticity. Findings are mixed, and several studies compare active wavelengths or combine light with other treatments.

Very low for benefit persisting after treatment ends. Follow-up after the treatment course is limited.

Rationale for the certainty assessment

The judgment is strongest for short-term wrinkle outcomes because two reviews and sham-controlled trials are available, but the pooled review combines varied protocols and scales, flags potentially missing studies, and contains inconsistent wording about significance. A blinded clinician scale was null while image measures favored light. The crow’s-feet result rests on one trial, hydration findings are mixed, and durability is poorly characterized (Jagdeo et al. 2018; Le Ngoc et al. 2023; Bragato et al. 2025; Park et al. 2025).
